Stage 3 · Grammar

Which form comes second?

When one verb follows another, the first verb decides.

Read these four sentences from two film reviews.
  • I enjoy going to see animated films with my kids.
  • He decides to set out on a journey.
  • She fantasizes about becoming an actress.
  • It really deserved to win the top prize.
What decides whether the second verb takes -ing or to?
When one verb follows another, the second verb has to change shape — and the first verb decides how.

English does not let two verbs sit next to each other in their plain form. Put enjoy and watch together and something has to happen to the second one: it becomes either watching or to watch. Which one is not a matter of meaning that you can reason out. It is a fixed property of the first verb, in the same way that depend is fixed with on and interested is fixed with in.

This is worth stating plainly because learners lose a lot of time looking for a rule that does not exist. I enjoy watching films and I want to watch a film express very similar ideas, yet enjoy demands the -ing form and want demands the infinitive. There is no logic behind that difference; it is vocabulary, and it has to be learnt with the verb.

Two shortcuts do work reliably, and they cover a large amount of real English. First: after any preposition, always use -ing. That includes prepositions hiding inside fixed phrases — the to in look forward to, be used to and get used to is a preposition, not part of an infinitive, which is why I’m looking forward to seeing you is correct. Second: to answer the question why?, use to + verb. He went out to buy tickets — never for buying.

A small group of verbs takes both forms, and it splits in two. With start, begin, continue, like, love, hate, prefer the meaning barely changes. But with stop, remember, forget, try, regret, go on and mean, the meaning changes completely, and these are worth memorising individually. He stopped watching and He stopped to watch describe opposite actions.

Before you look at the table: the tables below give the two lists of verbs and then the pairs that change meaning. Do not try to find a rule in the first two lists — read them as vocabulary.
Three groups, and three verbs that break the rule
GroupWhich verbsExample
verb + -ingenjoy, avoid, finish, mind, imagine, keep, practise, suggest, can’t stand, spend timeI enjoy watching thrillers.
verb + todecide, hope, plan, want, need, manage, deserve, expect, promise, refuse, seem, tendHe decided to leave.

Verb+ -ing+ to
rememberI remember watching it as a child. (the memory)Remember to watch it tonight. (the task)

tryTry watching it with subtitles. (an experiment)He tried to watch it. (he made an effort)

Look left, not right. The second verb has no choice. Find the verb or preposition in front of it and the form follows automatically.

The trap is look forward to. That to is a preposition, not part of an infinitive, so it takes -ing: I’m looking forward to seeing you, never to see.

The mistake to avoid. Not I enjoy to watch films but I enjoy watching films. Enjoy is the most common -ing verb in English and the most common place learners get it wrong.

Two shortcuts. Anything after a preposition takes -ing, with no exceptions. And worth always takes -ing: It’s worth seeing.

Full grammar reference — the -ing form and the infinitive with to

What it is

When one verb follows another, English requires the second verb to change shape. It becomes either the gerund (-ing) or the infinitive with to. Which one is not a matter of meaning you can work out: it is a property of the first verb, and it has to be learnt with that verb, like a preposition.

What it means, and what it does

This is a grammatical fact about English rather than a communicative choice, and that is exactly why it is hard. I enjoy watching films and I want to watch a film mean similar things, but enjoy demands -ing and want demands to. A small group of verbs takes both, and for a few of those the meaning genuinely changes — those are the ones worth memorising individually.

When and why we use it

English does not let two verbs sit next to each other in their plain form. Put enjoy and watch together and something has to happen to the second one: it becomes either watching or to watch. Which one is not a matter of meaning that you can reason out. It is a fixed property of the first verb, in the same way that depend is fixed with on and interested is fixed with in.

This is worth stating plainly because learners lose a lot of time looking for a rule that does not exist. I enjoy watching films and I want to watch a film express very similar ideas, yet enjoy demands the -ing form and want demands the infinitive. There is no logic behind that difference; it is vocabulary, and it has to be learnt with the verb.

Two shortcuts do work reliably, and they cover a large amount of real English. First: after any preposition, always use -ing. That includes prepositions hiding inside fixed phrases — the to in look forward to, be used to and get used to is a preposition, not part of an infinitive, which is why I’m looking forward to seeing you is correct. Second: to answer the question why?, use to + verb. He went out to buy tickets — never for buying.

A small group of verbs takes both forms, and it splits in two. With start, begin, continue, like, love, hate, prefer the meaning barely changes. But with stop, remember, forget, try, regret, go on and mean, the meaning changes completely, and these are worth memorising individually. He stopped watching and He stopped to watch describe opposite actions.

Typical situations

This pattern appears in almost every sentence where you talk about what you like, what you plan, what you have decided, what you avoid, and why you did something. It is unavoidable, which is why it is worth the memorisation.

  • After verbs of liking and disliking — enjoy, love, like, hate, don’t mind, can’t stand + -ing.I can’t stand watching horror films alone.
  • After verbs of wanting and planning — want, hope, plan, decide, agree, promise, offer, refuse, expect + to.He decided to set out on a journey to find the negative.
  • After a preposition — always -ing, whatever the preposition.She’s interested in becoming an actress.
  • As the subject of a sentence — the -ing form works as a noun.Watching a film with subtitles is good practice.
  • To express purpose — to + verb answers why?He set out to find the missing photograph.
  • After certain fixed expressions — it’s worth, it’s no use, spend time + -ing; it’s easy / difficult + to.It’s worth seeing it on a big screen.
  • After adjectives — to + verb.The plot is difficult to follow.
  • After look forward to — the to here is a preposition, so -ing follows.I’m looking forward to seeing the remake.

How it differs from similar structures

stop + -ing = end the activity · stop + to = pause in order to do something else. He stopped watching vs He stopped to watch are opposite actions.
to + verb = purpose (He went out to buy tickets) · for + noun = purpose with a noun (He went out for tickets). Never for + -ing to express purpose.

How to build it

Verb + -ing: subject + enjoy / avoid / finish / suggest / mind / practise / imagine + verb-ing
Verb + to: subject + want / hope / decide / need / promise / seem / manage + to + base verb
Preposition + -ing: … in / of / about / at / for / after / without + verb-ing
Purpose: main clause + to + base verb (= in order to)
AffirmativeI enjoy watching. · I want to watch.
Negative on the first verbI don’t enjoy watching. · I don’t want to watch.
Negative on the second verbI decided not to watch it. · I regret not seeing it. — not goes in front.
QuestionDo you enjoy watching thrillers? · Do you want to watch it again?
Passive forms…being + past participle (He hates being interrupted) · …to be + past participle (He wants to be told).
Perfect forms…having + past participle (She admitted having seen it) · …to have + past participle.
Common -ing verbsavoid, finish, keep, mind, miss, practise, suggest, imagine, risk, deny, admit, consider, involve
Common to verbsafford, agree, appear, arrange, choose, expect, fail, learn, offer, pretend, refuse, seem, tend, threaten

Spelling and word order

  • -ing: drop a silent -e (release → releasing); double a final consonant after one stressed vowel (begin → beginning); -ie becomes -y (die → dying).
  • British English doubles the l even when unstressed: travel → travelling, cancel → cancelling. American English does not.
  • Practise is the verb and practice the noun in British English; American English spells both practice.

Usage notes and exceptions

  • Verbs that take both with no real change of meaning: start, begin, continue, like, love, hate, prefer. It started to rain = It started raining.
  • Verbs that take both with a genuine change of meaning, and are worth learning individually: remember, forget, stop, try, regret, go on, mean.
  • Stop smoking = give up the habit. Stop to smoke = interrupt what you are doing in order to smoke.
  • Remember locking the door = you have the memory. Remember to lock the door = don’t forget to do it.
  • Try restarting it = experiment with a method. Try to restart it = attempt something difficult.
  • After make and let, the second verb takes no to: It made me cry, Let me see. After help, both are correct.
  • The to in look forward to, be used to and get used to is a preposition, so it takes -ing. This trips up almost every learner at least once.

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • I enjoy to watch documentaries. → I enjoy watching documentaries.Enjoy always takes -ing.
  • I’m looking forward to see the remake. → I’m looking forward to seeing the remake.The to in look forward to is a preposition.
  • He’s good at to cook. → He’s good at cooking.After a preposition, always -ing.
  • I went to the cinema for watching the new film. → I went to the cinema to watch the new film.Purpose takes to + verb, never for + -ing.
  • She decided to not go. → She decided not to go.Not comes before to.
  • It made me to cry. → It made me cry.After make and let, no to.

More examples in context

  • likingI don’t mind watching a film with subtitles.
  • dislikingI can’t stand people talking during a film.
  • planThey agreed to release it in cinemas first.
  • refusalThe studio refused to change the ending.
  • prepositionThe film is based on winning back something you have lost.
  • subjectComparing the book with the film is never quite fair.
  • purposeShe stayed until the credits to see where it was filmed.
  • worthIt’s worth seeing just for the soundtrack.
  • adjectiveThe plot is hard to follow in the first twenty minutes.
  • meaning changeHe stopped watching after an hour. / He stopped to watch the trailer.

A tip for remembering it

Do not try to find a rule — there isn’t a reliable one. Learn the first verb together with what follows it, exactly as you learn a verb with its preposition: enjoy + -ing, decide + to, look forward to + -ing. Two shortcuts do always work: after any preposition, use -ing; to answer why?, use to + verb.

Before you practise — the key rules

  1. The first verb decides the form of the second: -ing or to + base verb.
  2. After a preposition, always -ing — including the to in look forward to.
  3. To + verb expresses purpose; never use for + -ing for this.
  4. Not goes before to and before -ing: decided not to go, regret not going.
  5. Start, begin, continue, like, love, hate take either with no change of meaning.
  6. Stop, remember, forget, try, regret change meaning — learn these pairs individually.

Stage 5 · Main input

A film that travels

Why some stories work everywhere, and expensive ones often do not.

Before you read: some films are watched all over the world, and others never leave the country that made them.

What do you think matters most?

Decide first. Paragraph C answers this directly.

A film that travels

Some films cross borders effortlessly. Others, made with far more money, stop at the first subtitle. What is the difference?

AIn 2019, a South Korean film about a poor family and a rich one won the biggest prize in world cinema. Its director had a warning for audiences who avoid foreign films: once you get over the one-inch barrier of subtitles, he said, you will find many more films worth watching. The remark stuck, because it named something the industry has always known. Most films never leave home, and the reason is rarely the quality of the plot.

BNigeria produces more films than almost anywhere on earth. The industry there tends to work fast and cheaply, and it has an audience that stretches far beyond Nigeria: its fans log in from Brazil, India and the United States. Producers have learned to showcase African culture to the world rather than to imitate Hollywood, and audiences seem to enjoy watching stories they have not already seen a hundred times. A growing middle class looking for entertainment has done the rest.

CSo what travels? Not, it turns out, special effects. Distributors who study this say the films that cross borders most easily are built on a situation any audience recognises immediately: a family under pressure, a person who decides to set out on a journey, somebody who wants to escape a life that has closed around them. The cast can be unknown and the budget small. What matters is that a viewer in another country does not need to be told why the character is doing this.

DGenre helps too, but not in the way people expect. Animated films travel well because the voices can be replaced. Thrillers travel because tension needs very few words. Comedy travels worst of all: a joke often depends on the exact way something is said, and a translator who tries to keep the meaning usually loses the timing. Romcoms sit somewhere in the middle, which is why studios keep remaking them locally instead of exporting them.

EThen there is the slow route. The Shawshank Redemption failed at the box office when it was originally released in 1994. It has since become a modern classic, largely because television kept showing it and audiences kept recommending it to each other. Its story — friendship, patience and hope inside a prison — needs no local knowledge at all. Some films do not travel in space so much as in time.

FNone of this means a film must be simple. Audiences are perfectly willing to work; what they are not willing to do is work without a reason. A film that gives them a character worth following will hold them for two hours in any language. A film that does not will be switched off in ten minutes, however stunning the photography is.

Written for this course. Box-office and industry figures are drawn from published reporting on the Nigerian film industry and on international distribution.
